newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: Rescue work starts slowly after Madagascar cyclone.
newsitem.headline: Rescue work starts slowly after Madagascar cyclone.

text.p: Madagascar slowly mounted a rescue operation on Sunday after 100 people were declared dead or missing and up to 30,000 made homeless by one of the most powerful cyclones to strike the island in living memory.
Cyclone Gretelle first pummelled the Indian Ocean island's southern tip on Friday night.
The interior ministry's National Relief Committee (NRC) said the first medical teams and military personnel were due to fly to the area on Monday.
"The people need emergency aid such as medicine, essential foodstuffs like oil and rice, and building materials," NRC secretary-general Cecelien Aurelien told Reuters.
The relief committee met on Sunday in the capital of the world's fourth-largest island, Antananarivo. But rescue efforts could be delayed by poor communication and transport, Aurelien said.
Madagascar has a population of around 14 million. It is rated one of the world's poorest countries.

National radio, in contact with its correspondents in two southeastern towns, said 100 were dead or missing in its initial report on Saturday from the area but the exact number of casualties was still unclear on Sunday.

"For the moment eight are confirmed dead and 30,000 are without homes...But the death toll is certain to rise because the figures that we have are only preliminary," Rufin Rakotomaha, a Radio Madagascar journalist, said by telephone.

The journalist said six people died at Farafangana, 300 km (187 miles) south of the capital, where a swollen river burst its banks flooding the town. Electricity in the town was also cut. Two more died at Vohipeno when a house collapsed.
Authorities in Farafangana were forced to release all inmates from the town's jail after the prison building was damaged, the radio said.
Gretelle, around 600 km (375 miles) wide and packing 220 kmh (140 mph) winds, was the worst in human memory to hit the island's east coast, the weather institute and radio said.
Communications with the island's southern tip were cut after Gretelle swept through four towns in the southeast on Friday night and Saturday.
The coastal towns of Vohipeno, Farafangana, Vangaindrano and Manakara in the southeast were worst affected, suffering as much as 90 percent damage.
The southwest was also hit between Toliara port and Itampolo when the cyclone left the island.
Madagascar's south-east is a rural region depending on coffee, one of the island's leading exports. Most of the population lives in mud and grass dwellings in small villages.
At 6 a.m. local time (0300 GMT) on Sunday Gretelle was 450 km (281 miles) southwest of Madagascar apparently heading towards the Mozambican coast, the national weather institute said.
Toliara was flooded by tropical storm Fabiola two weeks ago. Gretelle was the seventh storm to hit Madagascar since the beginning of the cyclone season last October.
The country is still awaiting official results from its presidential election between former leaders Didier Ratsiraka, 60, and Albert Zafy, 69, after a run-off poll last December 29.
Church bells in the villages affected by the cyclone rang continually as bodies were pulled from the water, the radio said.
The radio said local authorities criticised the slow pace of a rescue effort.
"There is a total lack of boats bringing aid to the thousands and thousands of stranded victims," the radio said.
The interior ministry's National Relief Committee (NRC) said the first medical teams and military personnel were due to fly to the area on Monday.
The cyclone, the most powerful in living memory, hit a string of towns in southeast Madagascar before sweeping west across the island.
